en: *The Expanded Text on the Pure Land of Longshu*, Scroll One.
Composed by Wang Rixiu, Jinshi of the National Academy.
Having perused the entire Tripitaka and various biographical records, I have extracted their essential meanings to compose this work on the Pure Land.
This text contains not a single character that lacks a source;
I hope you will not disregard these words because their author is of humble station.
Desiring that everyone may understand together,
his words were direct and unadorned.
I am a native of Longshu.
The texts traditionally transmitted concerning the Pure Land are not uniform;
therefore, they are distinguished by their regional titles.
1. *Qixin wenzhu* (Essay on Arousing Faith in the Pure Land). Regarding the discourse on the Pure Land, it is frequently encountered in daily life.
Yet its remaining merit is only manifested after one's death;
those who do not understand take it to be merely a matter for the life hereafter.
Little do they realize that it is of great benefit even during one's lifetime.
Why is this? Because that which the Buddha uses to instruct people is nothing other than goodness,
just as it is with that which the Confucian teachings use to instruct people.
How could they differ?
Only their names are different.
Therefore, they take the Pure Land as their primary concern.
Thus, that which is manifested within the midst of daily life consists of what the mind thinks and what the mouth speaks.
In all that one does with the body, there is nothing that is not good.
Being good, one becomes a gentleman and a great sage;
in the present life, people will respect him.
May the deities grant their protection;
may blessings and prosperity increase,
and may your lifespan be eternal.
Speaking from this perspective,
who could say that those who follow the Buddha’s words and take the Pure Land as their core aspiration do not benefit during their lifetime?
Next, there are those who are deprived by the conditions of their karma and are thus unable to focus their will upon this.
Even for those who do possess such an aspiration,
adverse conditions can be mitigated from this point forward.
Wholesome conditions may be increased from this point forward;
as for unwholesome conditions, one should diminish them without ceasing until,
in the end, they are utterly severed.
Wholesome conditions increase without ceasing,
and in the end will inevitably reach a state of pure goodness.
Once evil has been utterly severed, [the mind remains steadfast].
When one's goodness is thus pure,
how could they not be considered a gentleman?
How could they not be considered a great sage?
Speaking from this perspective,
who could say that those who follow the Buddha’s words and take the Pure Land as their core concern do not benefit during their lifetime?
Furthermore, those next in rank do not know where propriety and righteousness reside;
they do not know that punishments are to be feared;
they esteem only power and status.
It is only the pursuit of power that drives one;
yet if one truly knows to take the Pure Land as one's heart's aim,
then one will also surely know to examine oneself and reproach one's own faults.
Although what they do may not entirely accord with ritual and righteousness,
it will nonetheless necessarily approximate them;
and although they may not completely transcend the reach of punishments, [they will still be guided by them].
They will also necessarily distance themselves from punishments;
gradually, they can escape the realm of the petty person and ultimately find refuge as gentlemen.
When an ordinary person possesses even a slight understanding of Buddhist principles,
the world will surely regard them as a virtuous person;
this is the efficacy [of such knowledge].
Speaking from this perspective,
who could say that those who follow the Buddha’s words and take the Pure Land as their primary concern do not benefit during their lifetime?
Some say: "One should follow the words of Confucius and take the teachings of Confucianism as one's core principle."
"Is it not beneficial to do so while still alive?
Why must one wait for the Pure Land?
He replied:
This is merely a worldly phenomenon;
it is not a supramundane phenomenon.
Worldly phenomena do not transcend saṃsāra.
The supramundane dharma directly liberates one from the cycle of saṃsāra.
Since the Pure Land benefits both during one's lifetime and after death,
it is of great advantage.
This is because it encompasses both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Second, regarding the arising of faith in the Pure Land: the two teachings on the Pure Land possess both theoretical rationale and historical evidence.
When one examines its principle,
it is seen within the midst of daily life and has never been absent from it.
This is what was stated in the preceding chapter.
As for its manifestation,
it is seen in the brief interval of a single morning tea.
It is not necessary to spend one's entire day adhering strictly to the method of ten recitations;
for there are nine grades of dharma-gates for practice,
and all people are capable of practicing them.
Even for those who commit evil deeds,
the Buddha does not abandon them;
if they turn their minds toward the good, they become virtuous.
Therefore, this Dharma-gate of ten recitations can be practiced by all people.
It is like a long-darkened room:
once a single lamp illuminates it, it becomes bright.
Therefore, even those who have slaughtered oxen or butchered horses can practice the Way by laying down their butcher's knives;
thus, for such practitioners, it is not difficult.
Furthermore, it does not hinder any worldly affairs;
thus, for those in office, it does not interfere with their duties,
and for scholars, it does not impede their studies.
For merchants, it does not hinder their trade;
for farmers, it does not hinder their cultivation;
for those in public offices, it does not hinder their service to their superiors.
It does not hinder monastics from practicing Chan;
indeed, all activities whatsoever do not obstruct one another.
Therefore it is said:
The practice of this cultivation requires no more than the duration of a single morning tea;
yet it can serve as a resource that remains indestructible for ten million kalpas.
Why, then, would anyone not cultivate it?
Suppose now there is a merchant who gains an interest of two coins for every one coin he invests;
he will surely rejoice at this.
One might think that one has gained much rest;
even a traveler who covers the distance of two days' journey in a single day will surely feel self-satisfied.
He considered that he had attained as much as was possible;
thus, having gained a small measure of something from external things,
he recognized his joy.
Or if one receives the price of one coin for two coins,
one will surely worry about it as losing the principal;
or if one covers the distance of one day's journey in two days.
One will surely worry about it, considering it a waste of time;
thus, one recognizes the anxiety when there is even a slight loss regarding external things.
Why then do I waste the limited time of my life?
As the sun sets and passes away,
the loss is immense.
Yet they do not regard this as a cause for concern.
The conditions for attaining the Pure Land are difficult to encounter;
it is fortunate that you have come to know them.
That he has attained something great,
yet does not regard it as a cause for joy—
this shows that he perceives joy and sorrow only in relation to minor gains and losses.
Yet they are unable to discern the most significant matters of gain and loss.
How can their lack of reflection be so extreme?
Moreover, this would not even require a moment of one's time.
The effort required is minimal,
yet the benefits achieved are beyond words.
Why would anyone not cultivate this?
If one does not practice at this time, how deeply lamentable! How deeply lamentable! 3.
Arousing Faith in the Pure Land: Three types of people hear of the splendors of the Pure Land all at once.
That many do not believe it is not at all surprising;
it is simply because they are constrained by what they perceive before their eyes.
Consequently, they assume that what is not currently visible before their eyes is likewise nothing more than this.
For instance, how could those who dwell in humble alleys and dwellings of filth and mire know of the purity of a grand mansion?
Those with small vessels who subsist on meals of coarse herbs and beans—
how could they know of the ten-foot square space before their meal?
Those with tattered chests who store but a few grains— how could they know of vast treasuries?
How could one know that the celestial treasuries are overflowing?
Dwelling in this defiled world of Sahā,
one fails to believe in its pure Buddha-land.
Therefore, they are born from a womb;
they do not know that there is the transformation-birth within a lotus bud,
nor that their lifespan does not exceed a hundred years.
They do not know that he possesses a lifespan as vast as the sands of the Ganges;
they do not know that his food, clothing, and comforts arise spontaneously.
They do not know that he enjoys the bliss of natural provisions and garments.
They are constantly intermingled with sorrow and affliction,
and thus do not know that there exists a singular, pure happiness.
Such, then, are the words of the Buddha.
One should not fail to believe something simply because it is not visible before one's eyes;
how much less so when the Buddha strictly forbids people from speaking falsehoods—
he would certainly never speak falsely himself to deceive others.
When people in the world speak falsely,
they do so either to seek profit or to avoid harm;
the Buddha has no such desires for the world.
What profit could there be in scheming?
The Buddha views birth and death as a blade cutting through empty space.
What harm could there be in avoiding it?
Thus, the Buddha has no occasion to employ false speech.
Among those in the world who are superior to the average person...
If he was still unwilling to utter false speech so as to ruin his conduct,
how much more so must it be for the Buddha?
His words are trustworthy.
There is no room for doubt.
Thus, the former sages said:
"If one does not believe the words of the Buddha,"
How can such words be trusted?
In the past, there was one who branded a loyal minister as a member of a treacherous faction and had it engraved upon stone.
Heavenly thunder struck it.
Now, it has been engraved and decorated with gold, jewels, and various colors,
and is enshrined within a wheel-store (dharmacakra-piṭaka).
The Buddha’s words state that one should make offerings with incense and flowers and adorn [the image] with divine dragons;
let his words be false.
This is even more egregious than the Stele of the Treacherous Faction;
why has Heaven’s thunder not struck it down throughout the passage of a thousand or ten thousand years?
It is because their words are sincere.
If their words are sincere yet not believed,
what else can they wait for?
Therefore, there is no longer any room for doubt regarding the teaching of the Pure Land;
moreover, from antiquity to the present day,
those who have practiced this have experienced numerous instances of spiritual response.
It is especially impossible not to believe this.
The "Responsive Resonance" (Ganying) is in the fifth fascicle.
Regarding the "Arousing Faith in the Pure Land" (Jingtu Qixin): some Confucian scholars may claim that the followers of Śākyamuni lack moral discipline (*śīla*).
To slight their teachings and,
on that account, fail to believe in the Pure Land— this is not so.
How can one disparage Laozi because a certain Daoist is unworthy,
or disparage Confucius because a certain scholar is unworthy?
Even the wise do not reject words on account of the person who uttered them.
How much less can one disparage its teaching on account of its followers?
Within the teachings of the Śākya, there are mundane dharmas and there are supramundane dharmas.
Those worldly dharmas that are identical to our Confucianism cannot be enumerated thread by thread; for now,
I shall briefly cite their principal points.
That which the Śākyas diligently teach to the world is nothing other than the prohibition of evil and the exhortation toward goodness;
yet how could our Confucians ever fail to prohibit evil and exhort toward goodness?
To speak of the present time:
the Buddha identifies killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct as the three karmas of the body;
yet Confucius speaks of overcoming violence and eliminating killing.
The poet says:
"King Wen’s virtue reached even to the birds, beasts, and insects.
How could this not be a warning against killing?
Theft certainly does not lie in what was said.
Confucius remarked,
"I have never seen one who loves virtue as much as they love beauty."
That a poet censures a lack of virtue yet delights in beautiful forms—is this not a warning against sexual misconduct?
The Buddha established four types of vocal karma: false speech, frivolous chatter, divisive speech, and harsh words.
Confucius said,
"If a person lacks trustworthiness,
I know not how they can be effective."
Is it not that one should refrain from false speech?
This refers to clever words and a commanding countenance.
"Scarce indeed is benevolence.
Does this not admonish against flowery speech?
As the Book of Documents says:
That you do not follow me openly but withdraw to speak against me behind my back—
does this not violate the precept against double-tongued speech?
Malicious speech refers to the sounds of angry outbursts.
One has not yet reached the level of foul language. Xunzi said:
"Words that wound others are more piercing than spears and halberds."
This has never been anything other than restraining the mouth from evil and anger.
Furthermore, the Buddha identifies greed, anger, and delusion as the three karmas of the mind.
Confucius, however, said:
To perceive this and contemplate its meaning is to restrain greed.
That is to say:
Boyi and Shuqi did not dwell on past wrongs;
this was precisely their precept against anger.
It is said:
"To be in distress yet not study—
such people are the lowest of the common folk.
This is a warning against ignorance.
From this it may be said:
Confucianism and Buddhism have never been different.
That which differs between them is as follows:
Only the Confucians stop at worldly dharmas;
the Buddhists, moreover, possess supramundane dharmas.
The Confucians stop at worldly dharmas.
Therefore, [the Confucian tradition] speaks only of a single lifetime, attributing it to Heaven.
Buddhism, however, possesses the supramundane Dharma;
thus, one knows that it spans successive lifetimes to reveal the beginning and end of the karmic conditions of sentient beings.
This is merely where they differ.
If one wishes to know the strengths of the Śākya school,
one must examine the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Amoghapāśa*.
If one has not yet understood the principles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and, failing to do so,
proceeds to criticize it, this is what Confucius called "acting without knowledge."
How can one not be cautious?
If this is truly so,
then the teachings of Śākyamuni may indeed be trusted.
How can one not believe these words regarding the Pure Land?
As for what is called the supramundane Dharma, there is even greater importance to the Pure Land;
one must strive in it without fail.
5. On Arousing Faith in the Pure Land: Regarding those in the five periods of the Dharma who are exclusively devoted to Chan meditation, they say:
"The pure land is but one's own mind;
how could there be any other pure land?"
"The self-nature is Amitābha;
there is no need to see Amitābha further.
This statement seems plausible yet is false.
Why is this? The Western Pure Land possesses both principle and manifestation.
Regarding its principle, it can purify the mind.
Therefore, all things are pure and sincere;
they constitute the land of the pure mind.
This is the case when considering their traces.
Thus, the world of Ultimate Bliss truly exists;
the Buddha has spoken of it repeatedly and with great care—
how could this be a false word?
Every person can attain Buddhahood;
thus, it is certainly not false that one's own nature is Amitābha.
Nevertheless, one cannot suddenly reach this state.
For example, just as fine timber can be carved into objects and images to achieve the utmost magnificence,
it must undergo the labor of carving before it can be completed.
One must not rely solely on excellent materials and thereby claim that the splendor of material forms is the ultimate;
this is what is meant by "the Pure Land is mind-only," implying that there is no further Pure Land beyond it.
To claim that because Amitābha is one's own nature, it is unnecessary to further behold Amitābha,
is incorrect.
Furthermore, it is erroneous to believe in the existence of the Pure Land while adhering solely to the doctrine of "mind-only."
He then claimed that the Western Land was not worth being born in,
asserting that through Zen meditation one could awaken to a nature that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs;
he further claimed that Amitābha was not worth beholding.
All have lost it. Why is this?
These words are exceedingly lofty;
I fear they are not easily attained.
In that Western Pure Land, there is no greed, no changeability, no anger, and no delusion.
Can my own mind be free from greed, changeability, anger, and delusion?
In that Western Pure Land, one thinks of clothing and receives clothing.
When he thinks of food, he obtains food.
When he desires stillness, he becomes still.
When he desires to depart, he departs.
When I think of clothing but have no clothing,
cold distresses my mind;
when I think of food but have no food, [the same distress follows].
Then hunger torments the mind;
when one desires stillness but cannot attain it,
the multitude of movements torments the mind.
If one wishes to depart but cannot do so,
then entanglements will afflict the mind; thus,
what is called the "Pure Land of Mind-Only" is indeed not easily reached.
That Amitābha Buddha possesses blessings as vast as mountains and seas;
his power sustains heaven and earth and transforms the hells into lotus flowers.
It is as easy as turning over one's palm.
One contemplates the infinite worlds as if they were right before one's eyes.
Even by the power of my merit, I cannot ensure my own permanence;
I fear that due to the gravity of my past karma, I shall fall into hell.
How much less, then, could I transform myself into a lotus flower?
If one cannot even know what occurs in the room next door,
how much less can one perceive the infinite worlds?
This is what is meant by the so-called "Amida of self-nature," which is truly not easy to reach.
Thus, my mind can be the Pure Land,
yet it cannot suddenly become the Pure Land;
my nature can be Amitābha.
Yet, being unable to become Amitābha all at once,
how could one neglect the Pure Land without practicing for it,
or abandon Amitābha without wishing to behold him?
Therefore, it is exceedingly easy to attain the Way by practicing in the Western Pure Land.
If one remains only in this world,
yet desires to engage in Chan meditation to awaken the nature and transcend both Buddhas and patriarchs, [the path is far more difficult].
This is already extremely difficult;
how much more so for those who cultivate the Pure Land not to be hindered by the practice of Chan meditation.
Why, then, must those who practice Chan necessarily disparage the Pure Land and refrain from cultivating it?
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"In the ten directions, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha."
"That Bodhisattva wishes to be reborn there;
what person am I that I should not wish to go there?
Is his fruit superior to that of all other Bodhisattvas?"
Speaking from this perspective,
the notion that the Pure Land is solely the mind and Amitābha is one's own self-nature is grand,
yet not essential.
To be lofty yet not practical,
or to cultivate without reaching the goal—
these have misled many people.
It is better to plant one's feet firmly on the ground,
engaging in recitation and practice;
then every person will surely be reborn in the Pure Land.
One who directly escapes the cycle of saṃsāra is as far removed from those whose words are empty and devoid of substance as heaven is from earth.
6. Generating Faith in the Pure Land: Generating faith in the Pure Land is because the Buddha’s eye perceives events throughout immeasurable kalpas;
from antiquity to the present, there is nothing he does not see.
Furthermore, it prohibits people from speaking falsely.
Because one does not deceive others with false speech,
and because one who observes the precepts possesses self-awareness,
one certainly will not boast of a self to others.
Therefore, his words are sincere and may be taken as a model for emulation.
According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it says:
There are ten kinds of immortals,
all of whom live for ten million years; when their lifespan is exhausted,
they re-enter the cycle of saṃsāra because they have never fully realized the true nature.
Therefore, they share the same name as the six realms of existence— namely, the seven destinies—
and are all people caught within the cycle of saṃsāra. Among the people of the world,
there are those who study the arts of the immortals.
Out of ten thousand, not one may attain it;
even if one were to attain it,
one would still not escape saṃsāra.
This is because one is attached to form and spirit and is unable to relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are merely delusive thoughts manifested within the true nature;
they are not reality itself.
Thus, a poem by Hanshan says:
"Even if you were to become an immortal,
you would be no different from a corpse-guarding ghost."
It is not like the Buddhist view of birth and death, which is spontaneous and free from all constraints.
In recent centuries, those who have attained immortality have been limited to none other than Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin.
As for those who studied the art of *zhong* (pitch-pipes), even among those such as Master Lü,
there were surely many thousands; within my own circle of acquaintances,
their number is likewise not small.
In the end, all shall die and be buried beneath the earth;
thus, the efforts and mental energy expended throughout one's life are spent in vain,
ultimately yielding no benefit whatsoever.
If you seek long life,
nothing compares to the Pure Land.
Those born in the Pure Land enjoy an immeasurable lifespan.
The attainment of longevity through this is truly great.
To fail to understand and cultivate this dharma-gate while instead studying the ways of the immortals is like discarding a magnificent jade treasure right before one's eyes.
Yet to seek after such a phony jade as the *wǔfū*,
which cannot necessarily be obtained— is this not delusion? Some say:
Question: "The Pure Land is something that occurs after one has closed one's eyes.
What proof or verification is there for this?
Answer: It is said:
The *Biographies of Pure Land Devotees* records numerous instances of spiritual resonance;
how could there not be such verification?
Moreover, those who are immortals have attained something.
Thus, [the teachings] were kept extremely secret and not transmitted,
for it was believed that to leak such celestial mechanisms (tianji) would incur sin;
whereas the gates of the Buddha-dharma fear only that they might not be propagated widely.
He desires nothing less than to deliver all sentient beings before he comes to rest;
his compassion is so vast that it is difficult to measure,
and is not comparable to that of the immortals.

7. Faith in the Pure Land. Regarding the seven types of people who do not believe in the Pure Land: there are those who do not believe in cause and effect, and consequently do not believe in the Pure Land.
Now, how can one possibly disbelieve in cause and effect?
The Sūtra says:
"If you wish to know the causes from a previous life,
it is that which is experienced in this present life."
One must know that the fruits of future lives are produced by what one does in this life.
If you do not believe these words, [you will suffer].
Why not observe this through the matters before one's eyes?
It is for these reasons that in human life there is poverty and wealth, nobility and lowliness, suffering and joy, toil and ease, honor and disgrace, longevity and early death.
Their fortunes and misfortunes vary in many ways;
although these are said to be the decrees of Heaven,
how could Heaven show partiality toward any individual?
It is because the actions performed by people in their previous lives differ that the retributions they receive in this life also differ;
Heaven merely presides over them.
For this reason, this body is called the retribution body (*vipākakāya*).
This body is born as a retribution for what I did in previous lives.
What room is there for the heavens to intervene?
For example, if a person has merits or offenses that manifest externally,
they shall receive rewards or punishments from the government offices.
How could the government offices ever act with partiality toward individuals?
It is simply that one presides over the principle that those with merit deserve reward and those with guilt deserve punishment.
How could rewards and punishments be imposed upon people without cause?
Even the government offices of this world do not impose rewards or punishments upon people without cause.
How much more so for the creative transformation of Heaven and Earth— how could they bestow calamity or fortune upon people without cause?
Thus we know that because of the good and evil deeds committed in previous lives,
Heaven and Earth respond with calamity or fortune as retribution.
Because they cannot be purely good,
they cannot receive purely favorable retributions; thus,
there are those who possess wealth and status yet suffer from misery and premature death.
There are those who are poor and lowly yet long-lived and happy;
there are those who are honored and favored yet distressed and humiliated.
Their respective karmic retributions follow exactly what they have done.
It is like a shadow following a shadow,
or an echo responding to a sound;
there is not the slightest discrepancy between them.
Therefore it is said:
"Plant peach trees and you will get peaches;
plant apricot trees and you will get apricots."
There has never been one who sowed hemp and obtained beans,
or sowed millet and obtained grain;
it is only that the time spent on sowing is brief.
The time spent in actual cultivation is very brief, yet the harvest is great; thus,
while the duration of performing good or evil deeds is extremely short,
the retribution for their resulting calamities or blessings is exceedingly vast.
Therefore it is said:
"In spring one sows a single grain of millet;
in autumn one reaps ten thousand seeds."
In human life, one performs good and evil deeds;
their retributions follow accordingly.
This is indeed the natural principle of cosmic transformation.
This principle is credible;
therefore, the teaching of the Pure Land must also be credible.
Why? Because both are the words of the Buddha.
Since the Buddha’s words regarding cause and effect are sincere,
he would certainly not speak falsely concerning the Pure Land; therefore,
it is due to a lack of faith in cause and effect.
Thus, those who do not believe in the Pure Land can have their delusions resolved by this. 8.
Regarding the Arousing of Faith in the Pure Land: there are eight types of people who see good and evil before them, yet see no retribution for them.
Consequently, they do not believe in cause and effect;
because of this lack of belief, they likewise fail to believe in the Pure Land.
They fail to realize that there is no instance where good or evil deeds have not yet received their retribution—it is simply that the retribution has not yet manifested.
It is merely a matter of speed.
The Buddha once said to Ānanda:
"There are those who perform good deeds in this life yet fall into hell after death."
"There are those who do evil in this life yet are born in heaven after death.
Ānanda asked,
"For what reason?"
The Buddha said:
"As for those who perform good deeds in this life yet fall into hell after death,
it is because the goodness of this life has not yet ripened."
The evil of a previous life has already ripened.
One who commits evil in this life yet is born in heaven after death is one whose evil in this life has not yet ripened.
The wholesome karma of previous lives has already matured.
That which has matured is the first to receive its retribution,
just as when one owes a debt, what is most urgent is repaid first.
The Master of Zuo says:
"Luan Wuzi possessed such virtue that he could provide protection for his son."
Therefore, although his son Yan committed evil,
he was able to escape calamity;
yet Yan’s son Ying practiced virtue.
Yet the wickedness of Yin led to his ruin;
thus, although Ying was virtuous, he met with calamity.
This has been discussed in terms of what is visible before our eyes in the world.
If the retribution for good and evil is already such as this even within the same lifetime,
how much more so across different lifetimes?
As the Book says:
"The Way of Heaven brings blessings to the virtuous and calamity to the licentious. Laozi said:
"The net of Heaven is vast and wide; it seems loose, yet nothing slips through it."
These three teachings all speak of this principle;
there is only a difference in its speed of realization.
How can one claim that because the retribution is not seen before one's eyes, it does not exist?
Consequently, one comes to disbelieve in cause and effect;
because of this disbelief, does one not thereby come to disbelieve in the Pure Land?
Regarding this, some have raised doubts, saying: "The Arousing of Faith in the Pure Land, Part Nine."
If a person here in this world recites the Buddha’s name,
how is it that a single lotus flower immediately springs up within the pool of seven treasures in the Western Quarter?
The preface states:
This is not difficult to understand.
It is, for example, like a great bright mirror: whenever anything comes before it, its reflection immediately appears.
How could a mirror ever harbor intentionality?
It is simply because it is luminous by its very nature.
So too is the land of Amitābha Buddha pure, clear, and pristine.
One naturally perceives and illuminates the worlds of the ten directions,
just as one beholds the reflection of one's own face in a clear mirror.
For this reason, one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha here.
In the western direction, a single lotus flower naturally grew in a pond of the seven treasures;
there is no room for doubt.
Yet some may still harbor suspicions, saying:
For one who recites the mantra of rebirth,
Amitābha Buddha will eternally abide upon their crown to protect them.
If there are immeasurable sentient beings in immeasurable worlds who recite this mantra, [the same shall apply].
"How could Amitābha Buddha possibly dwell upon each and every one of their heads?
He replied,
"It is likewise spontaneous."
For example, it is like the single moon in the sky appearing universally in all waters;
how could this not be spontaneous?
Yet some who practice with diligence may harbor doubts regarding it.
Furthermore, at the time of death, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas come to welcome [the practitioner].
Now, as for the immeasurable sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who practice with diligence,
how could they all know the exact timing [of each person's death] so as to go and welcome them?
He replied,
"It is likewise spontaneous.
It is like the sun in the heavens, which universally illumines immeasurable realms."
Is this not natural?
Moreover, how could the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power be anything less than that of the sun and moon?
Thus, it pervades and dwells upon his crown.
Since its period is known throughout,
what cause for doubt is there?

3. Universal Exhortation to Practice. Regarding the three types of persons who have never once died from the very beginning, the designation "death" is derived solely from this physical body.
Why is this so? It is because the spirit arrives and takes refuge in this [body];
its form grows from this point onward, and therefore it is called "birth."
Because the spirit departs and leaves this body,
its form consequently perishes;
therefore, it is called death.
This spirit is the self;
the body is the dwelling of the self.
Because the self comes and goes, the dwelling undergoes formation and destruction.
Thus, that which is born is not truly born;
it merely takes form through the arrival of the spirit.
That which dies is not truly dead.
It is simply because the spirit has departed that the form perishes.
People of the world do not recognize the spirit;
they perceive only the form.
Thus, they delight in life and loathe death;
can this not be considered tragic?
Furthermore, as for the arrival of the spirit—whence does it come?
It is because the spirit departs following the conditions of karma.

Universal Exhortation to Practice and Maintain. Universal Exhortation to Practice and Maintain: The human beings born within this world are all like bubbles upon the water.

"When that which hears and that which is heard are both exhausted."

that which perceives and that which is perceived are both empty.
When emptiness and awareness are perfectly complete, they reach ultimate perfection.

it is heard exhaustively that they do not abide.

Zou Binwang’s Dream of Awakening through Mindfulness of the Buddha. Regarding Zou Binwang, a scholar from Zhenjiang, whom I once exhorted with teachings on the Western Land: One night, while practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, he dreamed that he had awakened. He related this to me, saying: "Last night, while reciting the name of the Buddha, I suddenly felt as though I had awakened from a dream. I asked him what he had seen in his dream, and he replied: "In my dream, I saw myself traveling westward. After proceeding for some distance, I arrived at a place where the ground was level and smooth, and the air was clear and bright. There were no mountains, rivers, or trees; it was entirely composed of lapis lazuli. Upon reaching this place, I beheld a great city. Its walls were made of the seven precious substances, and its gates were adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, red pearl, carnelian, and emerald. Within the city stood a magnificent palace, its pillars and beams fashioned from the seven treasures. Inside the palace sat a person whose appearance was most sublime and radiant. His body was of golden hue, and his countenance was serene and majestic. He was seated upon a jeweled throne, surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas and celestial beings who paid him homage. As soon as I saw him, I prostrated myself before him. He then extended his hand and patted my head, saying: 'Welcome, good man! You have come from afar. I am Amitābha Buddha. Having spoken these words, he vanished instantly. I told him: "This is precisely the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. It is not a dream; it is the true reality. You should now exert yourself in the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, for the opportunity to meet the Buddha is rare indeed. Zou Binwang subsequently increased his efforts in recitation and, within a short time, attained a state of profound clarity and stability. He later passed away peacefully, facing west, amidst the chanting of the Buddha's name. This account is recorded here to encourage those who aspire to the West.

if you wish to attain long life, [you should do the same].
One should diligently refrain from killing.
If one desires wealth and honor,
one should diligently practice giving.
There are four:
first, the gift of material wealth;
second, the gift of the Dharma.
The third is the gift of fearlessness.
The fourth is the gift of the mind.
As for the gift of material wealth:
To bestow wealth upon others is material generosity;
to teach others through the path of goodness is the gift of Dharma.
The gift of fearlessness means that when humans and sentient beings are in a state of fear,

It is just as the grain consumed this year is that which was sown last year;

Thus, one cannot cultivate merit and receive its fruit simultaneously;
therefore, grain must take half a year to ripen,

Knowing this, many have cultivated the Pure Land and nurtured their roots of goodness.
Regarding the discourse on the longevity of the Perfected Person, I have heard it said: "The discourse on the longevity of the Perfected Person. I have indeed heard it.
The Perfected One said:
"In human life, clothing, food, wealth, and rank are all predetermined by the Office of the Netherworld.
If one practices frugality and refrains from greed, one may prolong one's lifespan."

yet if one indulges in greed and extravagance, ruin will be seen immediately,

Some may ask:

Those who are frugal and modest yet have short lives must have had few karmic allotments for rebirth.
If they were further greedy and extravagant, their lives would be even shorter.
Those who are greedy and extravagant yet live long must have had many karmic allotments for rebirth.
If one is even more frugal and modest, then [the lifespan] will increase all the more.

how could there be a fixed number of years for each person's allotted span?
All of this is merely the result of what was done in previous lives.
Therefore it is said:
"One must know the causes from previous lives."
Those experienced in this life are [the results of past karma].
If one performs many auspicious and virtuous deeds in the present life alone, then blessings and longevity will increase.
Therefore it is said:
"The spirits listen to this and grant you great blessings.
If one commits many evils in the present life, blessings and longevity will diminish.
Therefore it is said:
"One who frequently practices unrighteousness will surely bring about their own destruction.
Furthermore, for one who cultivates the Pure Land,
it certainly does not depend upon the abundance of blessings or longevity."
However, matters that diminish merit and lifespan are simply signs of meager virtue;
how could one not exercise restraint regarding them?
Matters that increase merit and lifespan are signs of profound virtue.
How could one not exert oneself?

all sentient beings, from the very beginning, [have been our kin].

it causes foul breath.
Therefore, one should not eat meat.
One will have many evil dreams;
therefore, one should not eat meat.
In secluded forests, tigers and wolves will smell its scent.

I have always said this.
In all instances of eating and drinking,

Mahāmati, all those who kill, for the sake of profit,

Various forms of killing,
slaughtering, and trading for profit,
O Mahāmati.

one may instead take a vegetarian meal.

if one acts in this manner, one may naturally prolong one's lifespan.
For example, eating vegetarian food in the morning.

there will be no end to them.

"If one wishes for the world to be free from the kalpa of weapons,

Should one not stand in awe of these words?
For those who cannot avoid eating the three kinds of pure meat,

Regarding the three kinds of pure meat:
that which one has not seen being killed.

The "bird-remnant" (kukkuta-maṃsa) constitutes one of the five kinds of pure meat.

Regarding food, drink, and sex—it is said, "food, drink, and sex": therein lie the great desires of human beings.
To regulate them as if they did not exist—
this is the way of the sage;
to exercise restraint rather than indulgence.

if one indulges without moderation,
one may become the lowest of the foolish.
Indeed, both of these are places where karma is created.
To slaughter living beings for the sake of one's own palate—
what is this other than the commission of sin?

If one wishes to exercise restraint over the mouth and belly...

for a hundred years, they become but dust in a single pit.
If one can reflect and contemplate in this manner...

Yao Po saw a Buddha image in the sky;
Tanjian obtained a lotus flower from within a vase;
Huaiyu received a golden pedestal to welcome him.
When Zhishun beheld the peacock flying and calling,
this was an effect of rebirth at the moment of death.
Zhitong saw five-colored auspicious clouds.
The Lady Li obtained three indestructible roots;
from the crown of her head, a youth emerged from the Treasure Treasury;
and for Duke Ze, a golden light appeared in the city of Luo.
This demonstrates the efficacy of what is shown after this life.
Those born in the Pure Land advance without ever regressing,
until they finally attain Buddhahood.
To exhort a single person to cultivate the Pure Land is to bring one sentient being to the realization of Buddhahood.
All who attain Buddhahood must necessarily deliver immeasurable sentient beings.
All those sentient beings whom he has delivered originated from me.
Therefore, the merit of one who exhorts others to practice cannot be exhausted.
As the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī said in verse:
To be able to exhort even one person to practice is more meritorious than one's own diligent cultivation;
to exhort ten or more people is even greater still.
Their merit is already immeasurable;
like one who exhorts hundreds or thousands [to practice],
they are called true Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, he can transcend ten thousand numbers;
this is Amitābha.
It is also said:
The affection between flesh and bone is difficult to sustain;
how many reach the harmony of white hair?
The vigorous and strong lose their lives.
Furthermore, there are infants whose lives come to an end;
if they are exhorted to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha,
they will be born by transformation within the pond of the seven treasures.
May we gather forever without parting;
may we enjoy longevity and happiness for ten thousand kalpas.
As an ancient poem says:
"Of all things that cannot be taken with one,
only karma follows the person.
The above is found in detail in the *Longshu Jingtuzhuan* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu) by Wang Rihui, in the section on "Exhorting Others to Form Karmic Connections."

Written by Dehae at Xingsheng Chan Temple in Jiahe City. Completed on the twelfth day of the ninth month in the year of Jiawu (1654), the third year of Wenlu, by Wang Hong of Youyun from Siming. Scribe: the monk Tuo Lian of the Kingdom of Joseon.
